Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.

Having overcome the divine power—the power of Lord Viṣṇu—which is the cause of bondage for His own portion, the jīva, and having conquered it only through His grace, he remains established in his own true nature, as Brahman.

In the twenty-ninth chapter bhakti-yoga is described in its many forms, together with the power of Time and the terrible course of saṃsāra, for the sake of detachment. Repeating what has already been taught, she asks in two verses about the distinctions within the path of devotion. Just as the characteristics of mahat and the other principles were explained in Sāṅkhya, so those characteristics have been stated by which they are in reality mutually distinct. That for which bhakti-yoga is the root and principal purpose has also been described. Now, she asks, tell me in detail the path—the various modes—of that bhakti-yoga.
By hearing the account of the various courses of transmigration, one becomes free from attachment.
Time is Your own form, the form of the Lord, possessed of immense power; because of it, and out of fear of it, beings perform what is wholesome and meritorious.

For one without sight—that is, for the ignorant—there is ego, the identification with the unreal body and the rest. His understanding is pierced through by and attached to actions, and he becomes exhausted. Thus the world has long lain asleep in the bottomless, unsupported darkness of saṃsāra. For the awakening of that world, You have indeed appeared as the sun who illumines yoga.
“Ślakṣṇa” means beautiful and pleasing.

“Paths” means particular modes. He states them: according to the path of the guṇas that have become one’s nature—that is, according to differences in their functioning—there are differences of disposition. “Bhāva” means intention. The sense is that devotion differs according to differences in the intended fruit.

“Having aimed at” means having resolved upon a particular end. “Saṃrambhī” means angry; “bhinna-dṛk” means one who sees difference. One who performs devotion with such a disposition may be of three kinds, yet all three are tāmasic.
“A separate attitude” means being one who sees distinction.

“Removal of karma” means the destruction of sin. “In the Supreme” means in the Supreme Lord. Offering to Him means offering one’s actions for the sake of Bhagavān’s pleasure. The injunction “one should sacrifice” means acting with the intention of fulfilling the scriptural ordinance. Seeing difference and worship of the deity-form are common to all three kinds. Thus within tāmasic, rājasic, and sāttvic devotion there are three divisions each, with each successive type superior to the preceding. Likewise each of the nine practices beginning with hearing and chanting has nine such divisions. Thus devotion associated with the guṇas has eighty-one varieties.

Guṇa-less devotion, however, is only one kind. He describes it in two verses beginning with “merely by hearing My qualities.” The construction is: that devotion in which, merely upon hearing My qualities, the movement of the mind flows toward Me, the Supreme Puruṣa, is the defining nature of nirguṇa bhakti-yoga. “Unbroken” means continuous. “Characteristic” means its very nature. It is causeless, free from pursuit of fruit, and unobstructed, free from the perception of difference.

By an argument from the greater to the lesser, he shows the desirelessness of devotees. Sālokya means residence in the same world with Me; sārṣṭi, equal lordship; sāmīpya, dwelling nearby; sārūpya, possessing a similar form; and oneness means sāyujya. Even when these are offered, devotees do not accept them; how much less would they actively desire them.

Why then do they worship? Because devotion itself is the supreme fruit; thus he says “that itself.” An objection is that attainment of Brahman after transcending the three guṇas is well known as the supreme fruit. True, he replies, but in devotion that result is merely incidental. “For My state” means for Brahmanhood.

In five verses he states the disciplines that produce devotion of this kind. “Properly practiced” means thoroughly performed. “Without motive” qualifies one’s own dharma, both daily and occasional duties. “Great” means endowed with faith and the other supporting qualities. Kriyā-yoga means the method of worship taught in the Pañcarātra and similar texts. “Commendable” means desireless.
“My abode” means My image or other sacred locus, and the practices beginning with seeing it. “With sattva” means with fortitude. “With nonattachment” means with detachment.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.
“With straightforwardness” means without crookedness or deceit.
The “disposition” here is the mind of the person who practices My dharma, the dharma of Bhagavān.

He gives an illustration of attainment without effort: fragrance has the wind as its chariot, its carrier. “From its resting place” means from the place where the fragrance resides. “Draws to itself” means appropriates or takes into itself. The mind described is even and free from distortion.

Because purification of mind comes precisely through seeing the Self in all beings, he criticizes exclusive fixation on the deity-image in seven verses beginning with “I.” Worship of the image alone becomes a mere imitation; alternatively, it means an imitation of true worship in the image. Disregard, neglect, hatred, and censure are prohibited in sequence by the following four verses.
“Having abandoned” means having ignored or neglected.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.
The ritual action is produced through material offerings. One who dishonors the aggregate of living beings is one who censures them.

Is worship in the deity and similar forms therefore entirely useless? No; thus he says “in the deity and so on.” It is to continue until one knows Me, present in all beings, within one’s own heart. “Performing one’s own action” means doing it as opportunity permits and without conflict with one’s other duties. By this it is also stated that this very realization is the limit and culmination even for one established in ritual action.

“Antara” means an interval or distinction. “Even” emphasizes the point, and “aram” means a little: the meaning is one who sees even the slightest difference. Alternatively, “antara” may mean “within,” and “udara” the body. I, as death, create fear for that person.

Therefore one should honor Me as having made My dwelling in all beings. The reason is that I am the Self of beings, their inner controller. One should see with a non-divided eye, that is, with equal vision.

checkpoint.source_note: This batch covers exactly 30 numbered verses. The Śrīdhara source groups 3.29.1–2 and 3.29.11–12. It explicitly gives no separate Śrīdhara explanation for 3.28.42 and 3.29.17 and 3.29.23; 3.28.43 has no text-bearing Śrīdhara block, so all four positions are marked rather than invented.

No separate commentary was invented for the four source-absent positions.
